subject: giant cuttlefish
title: Small Male Cuttlefish Dress as Females to Slip Past Bigger Rivals

scenes.text: Eleven males for every female. The small ones cheat.
Every winter, thousands of giant Australian cuttlefish gather off South Australia to mate. On average four males fight over each female; it can reach eleven to one.
The biggest male wins and guards her. So a small male changes colour to her mottled pattern, tucks away some arms, and reshapes the rest.
Now he looks like a second female. He drifts right past the guard, sometimes flipping between male and female looks ten times in fifteen minutes.
Researchers watched 62 attempts. In 30 of them, the disguise fooled the big male. DNA tests proved two of the impostors fathered eggs.
Sneaker males take about a third of all matings. The biggest fighter on the reef is guarding the wrong cuttlefish.

description:
Small male giant Australian cuttlefish disguise themselves as females to slip past the large males that guard them.
At the winter mating aggregation in Spencer Gulf, South Australia, males outnumber females by about four to one and up to eleven to one. A small male takes on female colouring, hides some arms and can switch appearance up to ten times in fifteen minutes; in 30 of 62 observed attempts the guard male was fooled, and DNA fingerprinting proved two mimics fertilised eggs (Hanlon et al., Nature, 2005). Sneaker males win about a third of all matings.
What other animal wins by pretending to be something else?
first_comment: A cuttlefish can show one pattern to the female on its left side and another to a rival on its right at the same time. Which ocean trickster should we cover next?
